```{r}
#| label: setup

results_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)))

openmx_lgcm_mgsem_mc <- readRDS(file.path(
  results_dir,
  "openmx-lgcm-mgsem-n250-results.rds"
))
openmx_lgcm_predictor_type_mc <- readRDS(file.path(
  results_dir,
  "openmx-lgcm-predictor-type-n250-results.rds"
))
lavaan_ar_panel_mgsem_mc <- readRDS(file.path(
  results_dir,
  "lavaan-ar-panel-mgsem-n250-results.rds"
))
lavaan_ar_panel_predictor_type_mc <- readRDS(file.path(
  results_dir,
  "lavaan-ar-panel-predictor-type-n250-results.rds"
))

method_order <- c("standard", "iterated", "MGSEM")
condition_order <- c(
  "dummy_only",
  "informative_dummy",
  "informative_continuous"
)

format_condition <- function(x) {
  labels <- c(
    dummy_only = "Dummy only",
    informative_dummy = "Informative dummy",
    informative_continuous = "Informative continuous"
  )
  unname(labels[x])
}

summarize_parameter_effect <- function(result, parameter, predictor) {
  selected <- result$summary[
    result$summary$parameter == parameter &
      result$summary$predictor == predictor,
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  selected <- selected[
    order(
      match(selected$condition, condition_order),
      match(selected$method, method_order)
    ),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  output_columns <- c(
    "method", "target", "mean_estimate", "bias", "empirical_sd",
    "mean_standard_error", "rmse", "coverage_95", "rejection_rate_05",
    "successful_replications"
  )
  output_names <- c(
    "Method", "Target", "Mean estimate", "Bias", "Empirical SD",
    "Mean standard error", "RMSE", "Coverage", "Rejection rate",
    "Successful replications"
  )
  if (length(unique(selected$condition)) > 1L) {
    output_columns <- c("condition", output_columns)
    output_names <- c("Condition", output_names)
  }
  output <- selected[, output_columns, drop = FALSE]
  names(output) <- output_names
  if ("Condition" %in% names(output)) {
    output$Condition <- format_condition(output$Condition)
  }
  row.names(output) <- NULL
  output
}

summarize_effects <- function(result, predictor) {
  selected <- result$summary[result$summary$predictor == predictor, ]
  methods <- method_order[method_order %in% unique(selected$method)]
  output <- do.call(rbind, lapply(methods, function(method) {
    rows <- selected[selected$method == method, ]
    data.frame(
      Method = method,
      `Mean absolute bias` = mean(abs(rows$bias)),
      `Maximum absolute bias` = max(abs(rows$bias)),
      `Mean RMSE` = mean(rows$rmse),
      `Mean coverage` = mean(rows$coverage_95),
      `Minimum coverage` = min(rows$coverage_95),
      `Maximum coverage` = max(rows$coverage_95),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
  row.names(output) <- NULL
  output
}

summarize_effects_by_condition <- function(result, predictor) {
  selected <- result$summary[result$summary$predictor == predictor, ]
  conditions <- condition_order[
    condition_order %in% unique(selected$condition)
  ]
  output <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conditions, function(condition) {
    rows_condition <- selected[selected$condition == condition, ]
    methods <- method_order[method_order %in% unique(rows_condition$method)]
    do.call(rbind, lapply(methods, function(method) {
      rows <- rows_condition[rows_condition$method == method, ]
      data.frame(
        Condition = format_condition(condition),
        Method = method,
        `Mean absolute bias` = mean(abs(rows$bias)),
        `Maximum absolute bias` = max(abs(rows$bias)),
        `Mean RMSE` = mean(rows$rmse),
        `Mean coverage` = mean(rows$coverage_95),
        `Minimum coverage` = min(rows$coverage_95),
        `Maximum coverage` = max(rows$coverage_95),
        check.names = FALSE
      )
    }))
  }))
  row.names(output) <- NULL
  output
}

format_tests <- function(result) {
  output <- result$test_summary[, c(
    "condition", "method", "test", "rejection_rate_05",
    "successful_replications"
  )]
  output <- output[
    order(
      output$condition,
      match(output$method, method_order),
      output$test
    ),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  names(output) <- c(
    "Condition", "Method", "Test", "Rejection rate",
    "Successful replications"
  )
  row.names(output) <- NULL
  output
}

format_iterated_diagnostics <- function(result) {
  output <- result$diagnostic_summary[
    result$diagnostic_summary$method == "iterated",
    c(
      "condition", "successful_replications",
      "ipcr_it_nonconvergence_replications", "convergence_rate",
      "mean_iterations", "mean_learning_rate_attempts",
      "mean_selected_learning_rate", "mean_elapsed_seconds"
    ),
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  names(output) <- c(
    "Condition", "Converged", "Nonconvergence errors",
    "Convergence rate", "Mean iterations", "Mean attempts",
    "Mean selected learning rate", "Mean seconds"
  )
  row.names(output) <- NULL
  output
}
```

## Overview

Simulation 1 used a total sample size of 250 and 1,000 replications per
condition. Standard IPCR was compared with iterated IPCR using analytical
iteration. The binary-predictor designs additionally included an oracle
multi-group SEM (MGSEM). Two model types were studied: an OpenMx latent growth
curve model (LGCM) and a lavaan discrete-time autoregressive panel model.

The current implementation returns an iterated-IPCR result only after
convergence. Therefore, all estimates, confidence intervals, and tests reported
below use only converged iterated analyses. Nonconverged trials are retained as
diagnostic errors, but cannot enter the inferential summaries.

## OpenMx LGCM: IPCR versus MGSEM

The two balanced groups differed only in manifest residual variance. The true
group difference was 0.2; all other LGCM parameters were homogeneous. The
oracle MGSEM estimated only the residual variance separately between groups.

The results were very good:

- All three methods completed all 1,000 replications without failures or fit
  warnings. Iterated IPCR always converged with learning rate 1 and required
  1.83 iterations on average.
- Standard and iterated IPCR produced essentially identical residual-variance
  effects: mean 0.19942, bias -0.00058, RMSE 0.05422, 94.1% coverage, and
  97.5% rejection of the null hypothesis.
- MGSEM was modestly more efficient. Its mean effect was 0.20065, RMSE was
  0.04769, coverage was 95.3%, and the parameter-level rejection rate was
  99.2%.
- For the five truly homogeneous IPCR effects, the average Type I error rate
  was 5.08%, with a range from 3.8% to 6.3%; mean coverage was 94.9%.
- The global heterogeneity test rejected in 92.1% of replications for both
  IPCR methods and 99.3% for MGSEM. The multivariate IPCR test pays a power
  penalty here because it tests all LGCM parameters jointly, whereas only the
  residual variance was heterogeneous.
- Mean analysis time was approximately 0.017 seconds for standard IPCR, 0.300
  seconds for iterated IPCR, and 0.190 seconds for MGSEM.

```{r}
#| label: openmx-lgcm-effect-table
#| tbl-cap: "Residual-variance group effect in the OpenMx LGCM."

knitr::kable(
  summarize_parameter_effect(
    openmx_lgcm_mgsem_mc,
    parameter = "residual",
    predictor = "group"
  ),
  digits = 4
)
```

```{r}
#| label: openmx-lgcm-test-table
#| tbl-cap: "Global and parameter-specific tests in the OpenMx LGCM."

knitr::kable(format_tests(openmx_lgcm_mgsem_mc), digits = 3)
```

Iteration neither improved nor harmed this simple binary-predictor result. Both
IPCR variants recovered the true difference accurately, with performance close
to the correctly specified MGSEM.

## OpenMx LGCM: predictor type and noise

The informative predictor was either a balanced dummy or a uniform continuous
variable. It produced a residual-variance effect of 0.2. Each model also
included an independent dummy and uniform noise predictor.

- Standard IPCR completed all replications. Iterated IPCR converged in 958 of
  1,000 dummy-predictor replications and 940 of 1,000 continuous-predictor
  replications. The remaining 42 and 60 analyses raised the intended hard
  nonconvergence error and contributed no estimates or tests.
- Learning rate 1 converged in 956 dummy and 934 continuous cases. Learning
  rate 0.5 rescued two dummy and four continuous cases; learning rate 0.1
  rescued two further continuous cases. The remaining failures involved
  inadmissible variance predictions or non-positive-definite covariance
  matrices rather than exhausted iteration counts.
- The informative residual effect was estimated accurately. With the dummy
  predictor, its mean was 0.20101 for standard IPCR and 0.20019 for converged
  iterated IPCR; coverage was 94.8% for both. With the continuous predictor,
  the means were 0.19913 and 0.19833 and coverage was 94.2% and 94.1%.
- Parameter-specific power for the residual effect was 97.5% versus 97.4% in
  the dummy condition and 61.9% versus 61.6% in the continuous condition for
  standard and iterated IPCR, respectively.
- Global power for the informative predictor was 92.7% versus 92.2% in the
  dummy condition and 39.1% versus 39.3% in the continuous condition.
- The global noise-predictor tests were well calibrated. Across conditions and
  methods, rejection rates ranged from 3.1% to 4.9% for the uniform noise
  predictor and from 3.9% to 4.9% for the dummy noise predictor.
- Among null parameter-specific coefficients, average rejection rates were
  between 4.7% and 5.1%. The lowest coverage was 92.6% for one coefficient in
  the continuous iterated condition, but average coverage in every condition
  remained between 94.9% and 95.3%.
- Successful iterated analyses averaged roughly 0.52 seconds, compared with
  approximately 0.02 seconds for standard IPCR.

```{r}
#| label: openmx-lgcm-predictor-effect-table
#| tbl-cap: "Informative residual-variance effect in the OpenMx predictor-type design."

knitr::kable(
  summarize_parameter_effect(
    openmx_lgcm_predictor_type_mc,
    parameter = "residual",
    predictor = "informative"
  ),
  digits = 4
)
```

```{r}
#| label: openmx-lgcm-predictor-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence diagnostics for iterated IPCR in the OpenMx predictor-type design."

knitr::kable(
  format_iterated_diagnostics(openmx_lgcm_predictor_type_mc),
  digits = 4
)
```

```{r}
#| label: openmx-lgcm-predictor-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Global predictor tests in the OpenMx predictor-type design."

knitr::kable(format_tests(openmx_lgcm_predictor_type_mc), digits = 3)
```

The converged iterated results closely matched standard IPCR. The remaining
limitation is algorithmic nonconvergence in approximately 4% to 6% of these
more demanding trials; the hard-error policy successfully prevented those
trials from entering coverage and rejection-rate calculations. The failures
were not completely random: standard IPCR estimated the informative residual
effect somewhat higher in failed than in converged trials. The iterated results
must therefore be interpreted as conditional on convergence, not as results
from all generated samples.

## Lavaan autoregressive panel model: IPCR versus MGSEM

This design used a balanced group dummy as the only IPC predictor. Ten model
parameters differed between groups. The IPCR Pillai test was compared with the
joint ten-parameter MGSEM likelihood-ratio test.

- All methods completed all 1,000 replications without failures or warnings.
  Iterated IPCR always converged with learning rate 1 and required 3.01
  iterations on average.
- Iterated IPCR and MGSEM were nearly identical. Across the ten group effects,
  mean absolute bias was 0.00816 for iterated IPCR and 0.00787 for MGSEM. The
  largest difference between their mean estimates was only 0.00129.
- Standard IPCR also performed well, but its mean absolute bias was higher at
  0.01509. Iteration notably reduced bias for several transition and innovation
  parameters.
- Mean RMSE was effectively the same for all methods: 0.12086 for iterated
  IPCR, 0.12090 for MGSEM, and 0.12111 for standard IPCR.
- Coverage across the ten group effects ranged from 93.7% to 95.7% for
  iterated IPCR, 93.6% to 96.0% for MGSEM, and 94.0% to 97.4% for standard
  IPCR.
- All three global heterogeneity tests had 100% power. Heterogeneity in this
  design was too strong to distinguish the methods by global power.
- Mean analysis time was approximately 0.028 seconds for standard IPCR, 1.69
  seconds for iterated IPCR, and 0.285 seconds for MGSEM.

```{r}
#| label: lavaan-panel-mgsem-effect-table
#| tbl-cap: "Aggregate performance for the ten group effects in the lavaan panel model."

knitr::kable(
  summarize_effects(lavaan_ar_panel_mgsem_mc, "group"),
  digits = 4
)
```

```{r}
#| label: lavaan-panel-mgsem-test-table
#| tbl-cap: "Global heterogeneity tests in the lavaan panel model."

knitr::kable(format_tests(lavaan_ar_panel_mgsem_mc), digits = 3)
```

This design supports the expected equivalence between iterated IPCR and the
corresponding oracle MGSEM for a binary predictor. Iteration reduced bias
relative to standard IPCR without materially changing RMSE.

## Lavaan autoregressive panel model: predictor type and noise

The informative predictor was either a dummy or a uniform continuous variable.
Both conditions additionally included an independent dummy and uniform noise
predictor.

- Standard IPCR completed all trials. Iterated IPCR converged in 990 of 1,000
  dummy-predictor replications and 984 of 1,000 continuous-predictor
  replications. The other 10 and 16 trials raised hard nonconvergence errors
  because the iteration entered a non-positive-definite covariance region.
- Learning rate 1 converged in 989 dummy cases and all 984 successful
  continuous cases. Learning rate 0.1 rescued one additional dummy case; no
  other reduced-rate attempt converged.
- Across the ten informative effects, mean absolute bias in the dummy condition
  was 0.01148 for standard IPCR and 0.00574 for iterated IPCR. In the
  continuous condition it was 0.00617 and 0.00535. Mean RMSE was very similar:
  0.12332 versus 0.12308 for the dummy and 0.20875 versus 0.20621 for the
  continuous predictor.
- Mean coverage across informative effects was 95.3% for standard and 94.0%
  for iterated IPCR in the dummy condition, and 94.6% and 94.5% in the
  continuous condition. Minimum iterated coverage was about 93.1% to 93.3%.
- Both methods had 100% power for the global informative-predictor test in both
  conditions.
- Global tests of the dummy noise predictor were well calibrated: rejection
  rates were 3.9% to 4.1% for standard IPCR and 4.5% to 4.8% for iterated
  IPCR. The uniform noise test remained mildly liberal for iterated IPCR, with
  rejection rates of 6.4% in the dummy condition and 6.6% in the continuous
  condition, compared with 4.7% and 5.0% for standard IPCR.
- Successful iterated analyses required approximately 4.1 to 4.3 iterations
  and 2.25 to 2.40 seconds on average. Standard IPCR required approximately
  0.03 seconds.

One nominally converged dummy-predictor trial warrants special attention. It
converged at learning rate 0.1 according to the primary criterion
(`C_SE = 0.0092`), but its per-observation likelihood change was `C_l = 0.5801`,
whereas the next-largest value among successful analyses was only 0.00025. Its
standard errors were implausibly small and both noise tests rejected strongly.
Excluding this single trial changes the reported aggregate results by at most
about 0.1 percentage point, so it does not explain the overall findings. It
does show that `C_l` can identify a rare pathological trajectory that `C_SE`
alone accepts. The subsequently added warning rule, `C_l / learning_rate >
0.001`, flags this trial and no other returned trial in the four simulations.
The nonconverged trials also tended to be more difficult samples, particularly
in the continuous condition, so these iterated summaries are again conditional
on convergence.

```{r}
#| label: lavaan-panel-predictor-effect-table
#| tbl-cap: "Aggregate performance for informative effects in the lavaan predictor-type design."

knitr::kable(
  summarize_effects_by_condition(
    lavaan_ar_panel_predictor_type_mc,
    "informative"
  ),
  digits = 4
)
```

```{r}
#| label: lavaan-panel-predictor-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence diagnostics for iterated IPCR in the lavaan predictor-type design."

knitr::kable(
  format_iterated_diagnostics(lavaan_ar_panel_predictor_type_mc),
  digits = 4
)
```

```{r}
#| label: lavaan-panel-predictor-test-table
#| tbl-cap: "Global predictor tests in the lavaan predictor-type design."

knitr::kable(
  format_tests(lavaan_ar_panel_predictor_type_mc),
  digits = 3
)
```

## Overall conclusion

The four result files are internally consistent: all scheduled replications
were attempted, failure counts reconcile with method-specific denominators,
and only converged iterated analyses contributed estimates and tests. They
provide a useful benchmark for version 0.4. Standard IPCR was stable and
generally well calibrated. Iterated IPCR matched the oracle MGSEM especially
closely in the panel model and reduced some standard-IPCR bias, while offering
little change in the simpler LGCM.

When iterated IPCR converged, estimation and inference were mostly satisfactory.
The remaining concerns are its higher computational cost, nonconvergence in a
minority of the predictor-type trials, a modest Type I error inflation for the
continuous-noise global test in the lavaan panel model, and the single lavaan
`C_l` outlier described above. The hard-error policy is important: it cleanly
excludes nonconverged trajectories rather than allowing unreliable fallback
estimates into the reported summaries.
